hints.quote: You will have questions on the exams that will be the ones that you'll see repeatedly through the years of what cusp are we talking about, you know, if we're doing a crown or if we're moving a tooth or whatever is there.
hints.take: "What cusp hits where" (the help sheet) is a recurring exam topic.

hints.quote: The bottom line is this, is that in an exam, if I use the term centric occlusion, this is what I mean, okay? I never mean, you know, the same thing as MIP.
hints.take: CO = tooth contact with the joints seated. Never MIP.

hints.quote: If I could have one wish as an instructor in occlusion to take my giant eraser, I would take the term centric occlusion and erase it from the world.
hints.take: He knows CO is misused; he tests the correct meaning.

hints.quote: MIP is a constantly updated position, all right? It is not going to be the same this year as it was last year.
hints.take: MIP is neuromuscular and dynamic; CO is structural.

hints.quote: If it's not specified that it's a Class II or a Class III, all right, assume always it's a Class I. That's always a safe way to go.
hints.take: No class in the question = Class I.

hints.quote: The only thing you really have to remember on fence posts is how to draw fence posts, okay, and what their canine relationships are.
hints.take: Draw the posts and know the canines; then use anatomy.

hints.quote: This particular slide, I'll probably only show it to you 20 million times before you graduate.
hints.take: The goals of ideal occlusion / mutually protected occlusion.

hints.quote: Yes, the closest determinant has the greatest impact, but that won't apply to all of our patients, because they just don't have it.
hints.take: Anterior guidance beats condylar guidance, when there is anterior guidance.

hints.quote: This is a left lateral motion, okay? That's a right lateral motion. This is a left lateral with protrusion. That's a right lateral with protrusion. Would I ask you questions like that? Yeah, of course I would.
hints.take: Name the borders of the envelope in each plane.

hints.quote: Almost every crown, almost every restoration I do, I seat the patient upright, does it feel the same?
hints.take: Contacts shift anteriorly when the patient sits up; check upright.

hints.quote: Whether it's clinically significant or not, that's a big debate, okay? We won't get into it. Want you to know what it is.
hints.take: Bennett movement / side shift: know the definition, not the debate.

hints.quote: An articulator is only really relevant when it represents the patient.
hints.take: Articulator size matters; know its parts.

hints.quote: So if I ask a question regarding what muscle is involved in what motion, it will come from this slide.
hints.take: Use the exam slide (Review → Joint and muscles), not other sources.

hints.quote: Now, when it comes to the pterygoids on here, I expect you to know which belly is doing what.
hints.take: Inferior LPt: opening and protrusion. Superior LPt: closing, disc.

hints.quote: I will say when it comes to anatomy, I presented it at the level that I would most likely test you at.
hints.take: Know roughly where each muscle attaches and what it does.

hints.quote: Although I provided you the innervation and arterial supplies and some of the slides on a few of the muscles, I don't particularly intend to ask questions about that.
hints.take: Innervation and blood supply: not tested.

hints.quote: The superior belly and the inferior belly, the lateral pterygoid, are truly different from each other.
hints.take: Different origins, insertions and actions.

hints.quote: Our disc is referred to as a disc because it is not a meniscus.
hints.take: Use "disc," never "meniscus."

hints.quote: This is a positioner, okay? It is positioning our jaw all the time, and it moves rapidly. It's the major positioner that we have. It is not a power closer.
hints.take: Temporalis = positioner; masseter + medial pterygoid = power.

hints.quote: We apply a little downward forces on the buccal shelf. Not a posterior force, because you don't want to push it back against it.
hints.take: Open lock: distract downward.

hints.quote: So the Posselt's envelope that we typically show you and ask test questions on and things like that is an idealized version of real data.
hints.take: Learn the idealized envelope; real tracings are messier.

hints.quote: We find that about 78% of our patients will chew on one side, usually the side that has the most stable tooth contacts.
hints.take: 78% chew on one side.

hints.quote: When we chew, we do know that we come back to that intercuspal position. And so it's like coming back to home plate when we chew.
hints.take: Chewing returns to MIP, not CO.

hints.quote: Tall cusp promote a deep stroke, flatter cusp, however we've got them, promote a more horizontal chewing stroke.
hints.take: Cusp form shapes the chewing stroke.

hints.quote: Our molars may be anywhere from three to five times the amount of force at the first molar than we have at the central incisor.
hints.take: Why anterior teeth tolerate off-axis loads.

hints.quote: Most of our chewing is on the second bicuspid to first molar.
hints.take: Supports the shortened dental arch.

hints.quote: Tooth contacts typically do not occur in speech. It's too rapid. It's too quick. If the teeth hit, there will be damage.
hints.take: No tooth contact during speech.

hints.quote: The incisal edge, when everything is rightly positioned, should hit right at the wet-dry line of the lower lip, okay? That's going to be clinically important.
hints.take: F and V place the incisal edge.

hints.quote: The visceral swallow is one of the things that may lead to developmental issues like anterior open bites.
hints.take: Retained infantile swallow → anterior open bite.

hints.quote: This is a list that you will see more times than you can count throughout your education of the things that you're looking for.
hints.take: Goals of modern occlusion = mutually protected occlusion.

hints.quote: When we treatment plan our patients, our first consideration should always be, do I have enough posterior support?
hints.take: Support first, disclusion second.

hints.quote: It turns out if you just restore to the second premolar, you can actually function very, very well. This is a concept called shortened dental arch.
hints.take: Shortened dental arch to PM2.

hints.quote: Anterior guidance by far is the one that is most important and the one that you have the most control over.
hints.take: The most important determinant.

hints.quote: They will need to be restored at an increased vertical, which means you're doing full mouth rehabilitation, regardless of their dental condition, which should raise a red flag to you already.
hints.take: Why neuromuscular dentistry isn't taught here.

hints.quote: It was called the rearmost, uppermost, midmost position, or RUM, and that's kind of what you needed if you were stored there. You need a good glass of rum because it's going to be uncomfortable.
hints.take: RUM was early gnathology's (wrong) CR.

hints.quote: Conformative occlusion... fortunately represents about 90% or more like 98% of the dentistry that we do in general dentistry.
hints.take: Most dentistry is conformative.

hints.quote: In the absence of those, then basically copying what's already present that's functioning and working for the patient in a helpful way is good dentistry. That's conformative dentistry.
hints.take: No signs or symptoms: copy the existing guidance.

hints.quote: The last thing you want to do is put something between teeth that normally should be in contact. MIP is teeth in contact, right?
hints.take: MIP records only where teeth don't touch.

hints.quote: Squirting impression material all the way around the dental arch or the registration material is dead wrong. It's totally 100% wrong to do that. Not for an MIP record.
hints.take: Full-arch registration = error (fine for CR records).

hints.quote: The tooth will stop and supererupt, and it never supererupts in a good contact.
hints.take: Never leave a restoration in infraocclusion.

hints.quote: The hinge articulator does not help you as the dentist ever... The advantage is entirely to the laboratory.
hints.take: Use an articulator about the patient's size.

hints.quote: I would not want all of my guidance to be on a Class 4 restoration. That would be a recipe for disaster.
hints.take: Class IV: share contacts with natural tooth.

hints.quote: If you do a four-unit bridge in the posterior, you just replace 50% of a patient's occlusion.
hints.take: Big posterior work: decide what to rebuild, don't just copy.

hints.quote: Typically, at a minimum, I would give three weeks if everything was very mild and asymptomatic. On a bruxing patient... sometimes go months.
hints.take: Time in provisionals before copying guidance.

hints.quote: Slide: "Remember this if nothing else… an articulator has best value if similar size to patient."
hints.take: On every objectives slide. A small hinge never follows the patient's arcs.

hints.quote: And this, if I could get one point across today, it was that one, okay? Your selection of the right articulator is going to make or break your time treating a patient.
hints.take: The articulator decides how much you adjust at delivery: chair time is money.

hints.quote: Non-adjustable articulators is primarily an advantage to the laboratory, not to you.
hints.take: Cheap, quick, small to ship: good for the lab, not for the dentist or the patient.

hints.quote: Why on earth would you ever use a non-adjustable on an anterior teeth when a semi-adjustable is going to move in the right direction?
hints.take: Teeth in the anterior guidance need at least a semi-adjustable articulator.

hints.quote: If I was going to leave any feature off of an articulator, I'd probably leave this one because, again, the average values are close enough to allow us to do good clinical dentistry.
hints.take: The Bennett angle is the less commonly adjusted setting; SCI matters more.

hints.quote: This is for the maxillary cast. That's what it's for. It is not involved with the mandibular cast, only the maxillary.
hints.take: Facebow = maxillary cast. CR or MIP records relate the mandibular cast.

hints.quote: 99.9% of patients, maybe 99.99% of patients, are easily treated with an arbitrary facebow.
hints.take: Arbitrary (ear-canal) bows are within 2-5 mm: clinically insignificant.

hints.quote: When you're hesitant to hand the patient the mirror, you've got a problem.
hints.take: Skip the facebow and you risk an occlusal cant in the esthetic plane.

hints.quote: The most common record that you will use is an MIP record. And I will suggest to you it is also the most misused record.
hints.take: Most common, most misused: the second most common cause of lab problems after a bad impression.

hints.quote: Probably the most important thing I can tell you is, if possible, don't use a record. Hand articulate always when you can.
hints.take: Use an MIP record only when the casts won't hand-articulate. The lab mounts with whatever you send.

hints.quote: Normally we would never want to put something on the occlusal surface of an unprepped tooth.
hints.take: VPS MIP records go over the prep only, trimmed to the cusp tips and off soft tissue.

hints.quote: I can't think of the last time I took lateral records doing full mouth reconstruction. As a prosthodontist, I do those. You know, I do protrusive records.
hints.take: Protrusive records are preferred: the lateral SCI is steeper, the protrusive one keeps restorations discluded.

hints.quote: So 3 to 5 millimeters is pretty good. I don't want to deviate to the left or right.
hints.take: Protrusive and lateral records: 3-5 mm. Farther out the Bennett angle reads smaller and the fossae come out narrow.

hints.quote: The job dictates the tool, okay, not the other way around.
hints.take: Choose by the patient's guidance and the extent of the work.

hints.quote: Anything that you can do in the laboratory that saves you clinic time is well worth the investment.
hints.take: His closing line: the facebow and the right records pay for themselves at delivery.

hints.quote: Slide: "Not on test" (Example Non-Adjustable: The UAB Handulator, developed by Fu and Givan in 2007).
hints.take: The Handulator itself isn't tested; the principle (accurate only in MICP) is.

hints.quote: If I turn around and I do a denture occlusion with bilateral balance, I would do the exact opposite. We'll cover that in the last session. Don't worry about that.
hints.take: How to set the SCI for a balanced denture comes in the course's last session.

hints.quote: That list will be a lot of your third-year course. Okay, so you will see those particular entities, but with the exception of one or two of those, such as local muscle soreness, and I will not go into a lot of detail on those this year.
hints.take: Asked whether each TMD on the classification list is tested: learn the general themes, not every entity. Local muscle soreness (myalgia) is the exception.

hints.quote: When someone says I'm being treated for a TMD, it tells you almost nothing, because you don't know what they have, and these things are quite a bit different.
hints.take: TMD is a collective term: muscles about half, joints about a third, each treated differently.

hints.quote: It will help provide an environment of healing that is helpful in resolving a lot of other disorders... that no way relates to saying that occlusion is part of the causality of the various TMDs.
hints.take: Occlusal treatment (a splint) can help without occlusion being the cause.

hints.quote: When we get over 3 millimeters, and some would say 4 millimeters, that's when we start to see an increased risk. Does it mean that you will have a problem? The answer is no.
hints.take: Orthopedic instability: 1-2 mm unlikely to matter; over 3 mm raises the risk; loading (bruxism) adds to it.

hints.quote: Here's what we know, is that we will see these both in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients almost in equal frequency. That's a very important point.
hints.take: Existing mediotrusive and laterotrusive contacts are as common in people without symptoms.

hints.quote: The practice of trying to equilibrate patients sort of prophylactically... as prevention of a TMD, is just not at all supported today.
hints.take: Don't grind existing interferences to prevent TMD.

hints.quote: We very much want to avoid putting in a mediotrusive contact because that's too sudden of a change for a patient. But if they already had one, then taking it away or leaving it there is probably not going to change their symptoms at all. Does that make sense? That's an important point today.
hints.take: Introducing an interference can cause problems; removing an old one doesn't help.

hints.quote: It's called protective co-contraction, okay? And there's nothing pathologic about it.
hints.take: The high crown: guarded movement to avoid pain, which then makes the muscles sore.

hints.quote: If we have issues of pain and dysfunction that involve motion of movement, typically... we're going to find those mostly involved with muscle things. When we're in occlusion and we still have pain and dysfunction, that's usually an issue with the joints.
hints.take: Movement problems: muscles. Pain with the teeth together under load: joints.

hints.quote: Hugely effective. It's hugely effective. Very, very important. And in fact, it was so effective, it led us to a lot of conclusions, thinking, well, occlusion must be the problem for a lot of these things. Not the case.
hints.take: The stabilization splint works, but that doesn't make occlusion the cause.

hints.quote: Because we see similar success, conservative treatments should always be our first go.
hints.take: Reversible and irreversible both 50-90%: conservative first.

hints.quote: A force is only traumatic when it produces trauma.
hints.take: Five factors: magnitude, frequency, duration, direction, distribution.

hints.quote: Pain is rarely, in fact, it's just not a symptom associated with tooth wear. It's too slow.
hints.take: Wear patients come in for esthetics, usually late.

hints.quote: Our clinical data is not really supporting that, and this is why we don't include this as a primary mechanism of wear, because we don't have the evidence to support that.
hints.take: Abfraction: shown in the lab, not confirmed clinically.

hints.quote: Occlusion is not an initiator to bruxing as once we thought, and that's just not the case.
hints.take: Bruxism is centrally mediated (sleep arousal, oxygen saturation, stress, medications, genetics).

hints.quote: The idea here is that you're going to brux against the $400 splint and avoid the $40,000 rehab.
hints.take: The splint stops bruxism only for a while; its job is to protect the teeth.

hints.quote: The vast majority have nothing to do with occlusion whatsoever. But... we can put something as simple as an occlusal stabilization splint and provide an environment of healing... It is not treating the etiology.
hints.take: His closing summary of the lecture.

hints.quote: So the whole goal of balance is referring to the tipping motions. It counters a tipping motion to tip it out of the mouth, and that's really what we're after.
hints.take: Denture occlusion keeps the prosthesis in the mouth; balance means resisting tipping.

hints.quote: What do I really want you to know from this is essentially, you know, what was the role of occlusion in this? And you're going to find out the answer will be practically none.
hints.take: Early dentures were made for esthetics; Bonwill made the first real attempt at denture occlusion.

hints.quote: So muscle control is likely to be the most important factor to keep a denture in place.
hints.take: Suction, adhesion and cohesion help, but they need good fit and aren't enough during function.

hints.quote: If you always remember this, all removable is movable, meaning that we always are going to have some motion in these prosthetics.
hints.take: Every removable prosthesis moves on resilient tissue; it is designed to resist that motion.

hints.quote: What I want you to know today is I want you to know that, one, that we have skeletal relationships that are class I, class II, and class III... And there's something called pseudo-class III that is related to the resorption that we see.
hints.take: The maxilla resorbs up and in, the mandible down and out: a pseudo-Class III, and teeth set over the ridge, in crossbite if needed.

hints.quote: If there are three things I want you to remember off this slide, it might be support, stability, and retention, because you're going to need it for the rest of your career.
hints.take: Support: vertical force toward the tissues. Retention: dislodgement away from them. Stability: horizontal force.

hints.quote: Of all the things that we need to address, stability is the most important. And it's the one thing that a dental implant is fabulous at.
hints.take: An unstable denture hurts and stops patients eating; retention problems bother them but don't hurt.

hints.quote: Maximum intercuspation is not really a term you use in a denture because their maximum intercuspation is a neuromuscular response, all right? And there's no neuromuscular response with this.
hints.take: In a denture: centric occlusion, with the joints seated (CR is easy to find).

hints.quote: That's why I like making these tables for you, because this table will basically give you the one how-to of how all this fits together.
hints.take: The balanced vs non-balanced (and lingualized) comparison: contacts, anterior contact, teeth, articulator. It is in the notes and Review.

hints.quote: I'm going to change the condylar guidance that I build the denture with on an articulator to zero, and my patient won't have a zero.
hints.take: Non-balanced: flat teeth, flat plane, zero condylar guidance, so the patient's own guidance separates the teeth.

hints.quote: Lingualized occlusion is hugely popular because it's much easier to arrange the teeth... it's most likely the one that you will do a lot of your dentures with.
hints.take: Long maxillary lingual cusps on a flat or wide fossa; balanced or non-balanced; no anterior contact (in class: never; the slides: difficult, can be compensated).

hints.quote: So the first take-home point about denture occlusion is that the denture occlusion is entirely based upon whatever selection we make to pick out that anterior maxillary mold.
hints.take: The mold chart engineers the mandibular anterior and the posterior teeth to match; the anterior mold is chosen on esthetics.

hints.quote: Do you think that's scientifically valid? And the answer is absolutely not. Does it tend to work for a lot of patients? And the answer is, well, yeah, it actually does.
hints.take: Berry's ratio (central incisor about 1/16 of the bizygomatic width) and ala-to-ala: not valid, but they tend to look good.

hints.quote: If I try to mark occlusion in the mouth by putting articulating paper, because the denture tips, as it squeezes into the soft tissues, everything marks. Okay, and it gives you the wrong information.
hints.take: Hanau's Realeff (resiliency and like effect): build and check a denture's occlusion on an articulator.

hints.quote: For dentate occlusion, we take those same principles and we turn them around and say, well, we use the same things to keep the teeth apart.
hints.take: Hanau's five determinants keep denture teeth together; for natural teeth, the same factors keep them apart.

hints.quote: Even the non-balanced flat plane are still clinically just fine, are clinically just as successful, and patients maintain great nutrition.
hints.take: Anatomic teeth chew a bit better, but it isn't clinically significant; chewing is one factor of many.

hints.quote: The more teeth that you have lost, the more I'm going to think about, you know, the denture kind of approach... The more natural dentition that remains, the more I'm thinking about the dentate type of occlusion.
hints.take: Partial dentures: many teeth left, plan canine guidance or group function; few left, plan like a denture.

hints.quote: I'm not really spending a lot of time on the anterior teeth, because the anterior tooth setup I'll go over in January.
hints.take: How to set the anterior (and posterior) teeth is the January denture course; know the principles here.

hints.quote: Slide: "No test questions" (on every history slide)
hints.take: The history (carved and sprung dentures, Washington's, porcelain, Bonwill, Gysi) won't be tested; keep the point: denture occlusion is about not tipping.

hints.quote: And then there's noncarious cervical lesions, which are in the same location, but it's a completely different etiology. Those ones are caused by factors that are not caries.
hints.take: Carious vs noncarious cervical lesions: the same place, a different cause. Carious ones are soft and brown, and resin-modified glass ionomer is a great option for them.

hints.quote: A lot of times we talk about these being multifactorial etiologies, like they can come from toothbrushing, which is an abrasion type lesion. You can have abfraction lesions, which are occlusion related, and then you can have erosion, which are acid related, obviously. They can be from one of these sources or they can be from two of them or three of them.
hints.take: Three causes, alone or together: abrasion (toothbrushing), abfraction (occlusion) and erosion (acid).

hints.quote: He showed that commercial toothbrushes used without toothpaste did not create noncarious cervical lesions. So he was saying that the toothbrush was less important than the toothpaste.
hints.take: The toothpaste matters more than the toothbrush: ask a patient with abrasion about their toothpaste.

hints.quote: The higher the number it is, the more abrasive it is. And the lower the number it is, the less abrasive it is. And so you want to obviously use toothpaste that have lower numbers.
hints.take: RDA (relative dentin abrasivity): higher is more abrasive, so recommend a low-RDA toothpaste.

hints.quote: We're using these soft toothbrushes, not just to prevent abrasion lesions. We're also doing it for gingival health.
hints.take: A soft brush protects the gums too. For pressure: brush more gently, or use an electric toothbrush with a pressure sensor.

hints.quote: So people that have toothbrush abrasion, one clue that it is from a toothbrush would be to see that the abrasion looks worse on their dominant side than on their non-dominant side.
hints.take: Abrasion worse on the dominant side points to the toothbrush (lesions on the left only: ask if they're left-handed).

hints.quote: So these are all pieces of evidence that point towards the fact that not all noncarious cervical lesions are caused by toothbrushing.
hints.take: People with leprosy who couldn't brush, archaeological populations, animals, and lesions on the palate and below the gum line.

hints.quote: Things are stronger in compression than tension... on the other side of the tooth you'd actually have tensile forces kind of ripping apart bonds... and when you have tensile stresses there, then that's when you can start to have these abfraction lesions show up.
hints.take: Abfraction: a load on an inclined plane flexes the tooth about the fulcrum at the bone; the lesion forms on the tensile side, just above it (the stop sign).

hints.quote: This is not treating TMD, this is something that's just a piece of plastic in between the patient's two teeth to prevent them from grinding their teeth, but to grind this piece of plastic as a sacrificial piece of plastic instead.
hints.take: For abfraction: a night guard, sacrificial plastic, not a TMD treatment. Its clues: exostoses and tori, opposing wear facets, generalized wear.

hints.quote: You tend to see that on the lingual of the maxillary teeth because the facial is protected by the lip and the lingual of the mandibular teeth is protected by the tongue.
hints.take: Vomiting erodes the lingual of the maxillary teeth, mostly the anteriors.

hints.quote: It would be a high buffering capacity, and that's bad. If it only took a little bit of your saliva to neutralize it, then that's low buffering capacity and that's good.
hints.take: Buffering capacity: how much bicarbonate (saliva) it takes to neutralize a drink. High is bad, low is good. pH is read with a probe; buffering capacity, by adding bicarbonate until the pH is neutral.

hints.quote: Orange juice and wine become way, way bad... Citric acid is a chelator, so that means it can like wrap around calcium.
hints.take: Ranked by buffering capacity, orange juice and wine get much worse, and citric acid chelates calcium: ask a patient with erosion about citrus drinks.

hints.quote: It's the amount of carbonic acid in there that determines its acidity, not necessarily its flavor, so bubblies are more carbonated and so they're more acidic.
hints.take: Sparkling water: more bubbles, more acid. Milk makes coffee less acidic, and tea is better than coffee.

hints.quote: pH is on a logarithmic scale, like I'd have to dump in like a swimming pool of water to like neutralize the pH, so that's why we just add in base, like a bicarbonate, to neutralize.
hints.take: Water only dilutes; a base (bicarbonate: a baking soda rinse, Basic Bites) neutralizes.

hints.quote: There is value in figuring out the etiology of the noncarious cervical lesion, because if you know what the etiology is, then you can do treatments to address it.
hints.take: Match the fix to the cause: a lower-RDA toothpaste, then a pressure-sensor brush; a less acidic drink and bicarbonate; a night guard.

hints.quote: If they're cleansable and they don't hurt and they don't look ugly and they're not near the pulp, or they're not very deep... then I wouldn't necessarily need to [restore them].
hints.take: Restore an NCCL when it can't be cleaned, hurts, looks bad or is deep, near the pulp (what he learned in school, "not official").

hints.quote: I measured the pH of all these different mouth rinses... you rinse your mouth for like 30 seconds, maybe twice a day. So that's probably not that big of a deal.
hints.take: Low-pH mouth rinses: probably not a big deal.

hints.quote: These are all kind of wives' tales that I don't know that there's evidence for, but they make sense.
hints.take: Acidic drinks only at mealtimes, a straw, a water rinse afterward: sensible, but unproven.

hints.quote: It's injury resulting in tissue changes within the periodontal attachment apparatus as a result of occlusal forces. So the initiating factor here is the occlusal force, and the injury that results in the periodontium is what we call occlusal trauma.
hints.take: Occlusal trauma is the injury, not the force: the force starts it, the tissue changes in the periodontium are the trauma.

hints.quote: We call that primary occlusal trauma because the tooth has not lost a single ounce or millimeter of... attachment or bone.
hints.take: Primary: traumatic forces on normal support (no bone or attachment lost).

hints.quote: So normal or traumatic occlusal forces, when they're applied to a tooth or a number of teeth that have a reduced periodontal support.
hints.take: Secondary: normal or traumatic forces on reduced support. The fence post: less of it in the ground, the same lean tips it.

hints.quote: The distinction between the two is simply clinical... But when you look at what the injury caused histologically, it's going to be exactly the same, whether it's primary or secondary.
hints.take: Primary vs secondary is clinical; histologically the same.

hints.quote: Because the tooth is being moved in both directions, it creates this hourglass shape that you see here around the tooth. That means you have a widened PDL, you have some bone loss on either side or on both sides.
hints.take: Jiggling forces: from both sides, an hourglass-shaped widening of the PDL. Orthodontics uses a controlled unilateral force.

hints.quote: The trauma itself can be only confirmed histologically. So when we look at signs clinical and radiographic, these are surrogate to those histological findings.
hints.take: Confirmed only histologically; the signs are surrogates. A diagnosis, not a finding.

hints.quote: Fremitus means it's a palpable or visible movement of a tooth when subjected to occlusal forces.
hints.take: Fremitus: the patient taps, a finger on the facial gingiva feels the tooth move. Not a mobility grade, but usually a Class 3 tooth.

hints.quote: The space generally in health is roughly 0.25 millimeter... widened PDL space is telling us that this tooth is probably under some forces that are making it shift in multiple directions.
hints.take: Radiographic signs: a widened PDL (normal about 0.25 mm), a thickened or discontinued lamina dura, bone loss, root resorption.

hints.quote: Just because you see a vertical defect around the tooth, do not assume there's occlusal trauma. This is not a cause and effect type thing.
hints.take: A vertical defect doesn't mean occlusal trauma (trauma with bone loss tends to be vertical, not the reverse).

hints.quote: Mobility is not a bad thing. So if you saw a tooth with class 2 mobility, do not assume that this tooth now has a hopeless prognosis.
hints.take: Mobility can be adaptation: find out why. Class 2 isn't hopeless; Class 3 is much worse.

hints.quote: It's been shown that mobile teeth respond less well to treatment, whether it's regenerative treatment... or whether it's soft tissue grafting.
hints.take: Mobile teeth heal less well: bring a Class 2 tooth to Class 1 or less by adjusting the occlusion if you can.

hints.quote: All we know is that you do this occlusal damage, things will get bad, but if you stop it in time, things will get stable back again.
hints.take: Animals, trauma alone: mobility and less dense bone, no attachment loss, reversible once stopped. Not a primary factor.

hints.quote: That tells us that just stopping the occlusal trauma is not going to reverse periodontitis if you already have it in place.
hints.take: Stopping the trauma doesn't reverse periodontitis: treat the periodontitis.

hints.quote: Except in those acute conditions, treatment is usually first addressed... following efforts to reduce or minimize the inflammatory lesion.
hints.take: Adjust the occlusion after treating the inflammation (at re-evaluation), unless it's acute, like fremitus at the first exam.

hints.quote: So occlusal trauma alone does not cause gingivitis or periodontitis. Does it have an effect on the periodontal tissues? The answer is absolutely yes.
hints.take: His bottom line: trauma doesn't cause gingivitis or periodontitis, but it affects the supporting tissues.

hints.quote: You will not see loss of bone height if you only have occlusal trauma. And these changes are reversible once you control the occlusal trauma of the tooth.
hints.take: Trauma alone: bone resorbs in density, not height, and it reverses once the force is gone.

hints.quote: Occlusal adjustment may reduce the mobility of traumatized teeth and promote regrowth of bone, but it will not arrest the rate of further breakdown caused by microbial plaque.
hints.take: Adjustment helps mobility and bone, but only plaque control stops the disease.

hints.quote: When performed, adjustment of occlusal discrepancies should follow successful anti-infective periodontal therapy.
hints.take: Treat the infection first, then adjust (an adjunct, like antibiotics).

hints.quote: Don't go in the weeds about it... But you don't need to learn all the names and such. Conclusions are enough.
hints.take: The researchers' names and the studies' details (Glickman, Waerhaug, the Rochester and Gothenburg groups): not needed. Learn the conclusions.
